The text focuses on the Picard variety of a proper scheme defined over a perfect field. In this setting, the Picard variety is an important algebraic group that encodes information about line bundles on the scheme, especially those that are algebraically equivalent to zero. Studying this variety provides insight into both the geometry of the scheme and the algebraic group structures naturally associated with it.

A central part of the discussion is the description of the maximal torus of the Picard variety. The maximal torus is the largest subgroup of multiplicative type contained in the relevant algebraic group. Its structure reflects the “toric” part of the Picard variety and is closely related to discrete and combinatorial features of the underlying scheme. Understanding this torus helps separate the multiplicative components of the Picard variety from its other algebraic parts.

The text also describes the maximal unipotent subgroup associated with the Picard variety. This subgroup captures the unipotent, or additive, part of the algebraic group structure. In positive characteristic, such unipotent components can play a particularly significant role, and their behavior often reflects subtle geometric properties of the scheme. Identifying and analyzing the maximal unipotent subgroup therefore gives a more refined picture of the Picard variety’s internal structure.

Overall, the work concerns the structural aspects of algebraic groups arising from Picard varieties. By examining both the maximal torus and the maximal unipotent subgroup, it aims to clarify how the Picard variety decomposes into different algebraic components. This contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between the geometry of proper schemes over perfect fields and the algebraic groups naturally attached to them.

This work studies the internal structure of the Picard variety associated with a proper scheme over a perfect field. The Picard variety is a fundamental object in algebraic geometry: it encodes families of line bundles on the scheme and reflects important geometric information about the underlying space. In this setting, the paper focuses on describing two central components of its algebraic group structure: the maximal torus and the maximal unipotent subgroup.

The main contribution is an explicit identification of these subgroup components. The maximal torus captures the multiplicative, diagonalizable part of the Picard variety, while the maximal unipotent subgroup accounts for its unipotent or additive-type behavior. By determining these pieces, the work gives a clearer description of how the Picard variety decomposes into its basic algebraic constituents.

This analysis is particularly useful because the Picard variety of a proper scheme need not be an abelian variety in the classical sense; it may contain additional affine parts, including toric and unipotent components. Understanding these components helps clarify how singularities, nonreduced structures, or other geometric features of the scheme influence the Picard variety. Thus, the results provide a structural description of the Picard variety over a perfect field and contribute to a more detailed understanding of the relationship between the geometry of a scheme and the algebraic properties of its Picard functor.

Picard is a name associated with exploration, intelligence, and leadership. For many people, the word immediately brings to mind **Jean-Luc Picard**, the famous captain from *Star Trek: The Next Generation*. As commander of the starship Enterprise, Picard represents diplomacy, curiosity, courage, and a deep respect for knowledge. Unlike leaders who rely mainly on force, Picard often solves problems through conversation, patience, and moral judgment.

The name Picard also has other meanings. It can refer to **Picardy**, a historical region in northern France, whose people and culture are sometimes described as Picard. In science and mathematics, the name appears in connection with figures such as **Émile Picard**, a French mathematician known for important work in analysis and differential equations.

Whether in fiction, history, or science, Picard suggests a connection to discovery and thought. It is a name that can represent both the human desire to explore new worlds and the intellectual effort to understand them.

This project studies the structure of Picard varieties \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/k}\) associated to proper schemes \(X\) over a perfect field \(k\), with particular emphasis on the affine part in the Chevalley decomposition. While the reduced identity component of the Picard scheme is an extension of an abelian variety by a connected affine algebraic group, the latter may contain both toric and unipotent factors, especially when \(X\) is singular or non-normal.

The main goal is to relate these toric and unipotent parts to explicit geometric and cohomological invariants of \(X\). The toric component is expected to reflect combinatorial phenomena such as the incidence structure of irreducible components, conductor data, or the dual complex of a normalization, while the unipotent component is tied to infinitesimal and non-reduced features, including failures of seminormality and contributions from nilpotents or inseparable phenomena in positive characteristic.

A central theme is to use normalization, conductor squares, and descent for line bundles to express \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/k}\) in terms of more accessible pieces. This leads to exact sequences comparing the Picard varieties of \(X\), its normalization, and conductor subschemes. The project aims to isolate criteria under which the affine part is purely toric, purely unipotent, or trivial, and to compute its dimension and structure in concrete classes of examples, such as reducible curves, seminormal schemes, and singular surfaces.

Overall, the work seeks a clearer geometric interpretation of the non-abelian part of the Picard variety, refining the relationship between singularities of \(X\) and the algebraic group structure of \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{X/k}\).
